I've been spending some time researching how AI agents could change the way we shop and interact with online businesses, and one question keeps coming up: what happens when AI agents become the customers?

While exploring this, I came across a presentation by GOAT Network CEO Kevin Liu at KBW 2026, titled "Your Next Customer Is an AI Agent."

I spent about 20 minutes watching it, and it helped me understand something I hadn't given much thought to before. The technology for AI agents to discover products and make purchases is already taking shape, but are online businesses actually prepared to sell to them?

Kevin's presentation made that gap particularly clear.

According to the data he shared, agent traffic to business websites has increased 4x. With Meta Muse, Manus 2.0 and ChatGPT shopping features entering the picture, AI-powered buyers are already finding their way into commerce. McKinsey also estimates that this could become a $3–5 trillion economy by 2030.

The buying process itself is becoming straightforward. You tell your agent what you want, it finds the product, asks for permission, makes the payment and gets a receipt.

But here's the problem: the merchant side isn't ready.

Right now, when you ask ChatGPT to buy something, it often relies on highly ranked websites or merchants within its existing partnerships. This creates a serious discovery problem for smaller businesses, whether they're in Korea, elsewhere in Asia or anywhere around the world.

Their products might be available online, but if AI agents cannot properly discover and interact with their stores, they're practically invisible to this new category of buyers.

That's the gap Kevin explained how GOAT Network intends to address, and the interesting thing is that it isn't built around just one product. It's an entire stack.

At the foundation is Bitcoin settlement. If machines are going to transact with other machines at an enormous scale, the underlying settlement layer needs to be secure and reliable. GOAT Network builds on Ziren ZKVM and BitVM3, with transactions ultimately settling on Bitcoin.

The next layer deals with wallets and payment mandates. GOAT integrates with protocols like x402 and MPP, allowing agents to pay from different chains without requiring users to bridge their funds first. There's also a mandate layer that lets users define spending permissions, budgets and what happens when a transaction fails.

Then comes the part merchants can actually use: GOAT Flow.

This was particularly interesting because I got to test it after the presentation, and the process is as straightforward as Kevin described.

You register with basic details, including your name and business description, choose how you want to receive payments, add your product and set a price. GOAT Flow supports card payments through Stripe, including Visa, Mastercard, Amex and JCB, alongside crypto payments across 10 chains.

Once you're done, it generates a page with a dedicated FOR AGENTS section. Humans can browse the regular product information, while AI agents can read the structured details they need to understand and purchase what's being offered.

And you don't need to write any code to get started.

They also demonstrated this at Booth 37 during KBW, where visitors could watch live AI agents purchase real mascots and gift cards. Out of the 450 people who tried it, 310 purchases were completed through an agent, with many participants making their first-ever purchase using an AI agent.

Kevin also shared some interesting details about GOAT's plans in Korea. Founded in Silicon Valley in 2023, the team now has offices in San Francisco, Toronto and Seoul, and has been building in Korea for three years.

He mentioned that GOAT plans to announce its first Korean investment soon and wants to work with local partners on Korean stablecoins, recognising that local merchants need payment solutions that fit the markets they operate in.

One line from the presentation stayed with me:

"Your next customer is an AI agent, that's for sure."

And the more I think about it, the more sense it makes. Online businesses have spent years making their websites accessible to people, but the next stage of commerce will require them to make their products discoverable, understandable and payable by AI agents too.

If your store isn't ready for that transition, it's worth paying attention to what's happening now.

How much can you trust OpenAI Dots, Grok Bots or Meta Muse? I did not want to wait for Claude Duet. So I am building my own.

Meet Dragonfly 🪽, a personal email assistant that lives on my Mac mini, not in someone else’s cloud.

What it does:
📬 Watches the Gmail and Apple Mail folders I point it at, on my schedule
🧠 Remembers people and conversations in an Obsidian vault I can read and edit
✍️ Drafts replies when someone is waiting on me
📱 Tells me on Telegram what needs me

What it can’t do is the part I care about most:
🔒 It can’t send anything unless I reply “send” to that exact draft. Sending is plain code, not AI.
🛡️ An email can’t give it orders. Everything it reads is treated as information, never as instructions.
🚧 A gate checks every single tool call. If it has read outside text, it can’t change its own rules, and those changes wait for my OK.
↩️ Every run is saved in its memory’s history, and I can undo any change with one click.

Built with Claude Code, Python, Swift and a lot of “what could go wrong here?”

Would you let an AI assistant into your inbox? What would it need to earn your trust? 👇
